vignette:
Sergeant Elena Reyes speaks of the sky with a wariness once reserved for enemy combatants. Before the hurricane, she tells me, she loved a good thunderstorm. She'd sit on the porch with her husband, Marco, and watch the clouds gather, finding a strange peace in the raw power of it all. Now, she keeps three different weather apps on her phone, and the notification of a severe weather watch is enough to make her heart hammer against her ribs.

The storm that changed everything wasn't overseas in a desert she'd been trained for; it was here, at home. Her National Guard unit was activated days before landfall, tasked with staging equipment and preparing for the aftermath. Elena, a logistics NCO for nearly fifteen years, was in her element. Her world was one of lists, schedules, and accountability. She knew where every generator, every case of MREs, and every roll of concertina wire was supposed to be. Control was her craft.

Then the storm hit with a fury that defied all forecasts. Her unit was hunkered down in a concrete armory, a building designed to withstand almost anything. But the water began to rise, first seeping under the bay doors, then pouring through compromised window seals. The lights flickered and died, plunging them into a terrifying darkness punctuated only by the scream of the wind and the sickening groan of the roof. For thirty-six hours, she and her soldiers were trapped. The water rose to their waists. She remembers the cold, the smell of mud and sewage, and the constant, vibrating fear that the building would collapse. Her training was useless against the rising tide. All she could do was keep her younger, terrified soldiers calm, her voice a steady beacon in the roaring dark, even as her own control dissolved into a primal need to survive.

When the water finally receded and they were able to force the doors open, the world she knew was gone. Her training kicked back in immediately. The Sergeant took over where the woman had fractured. For the next two weeks, she worked tirelessly, coordinating rescue efforts, distributing food and water, and moving through the wreckage of her own community. She saw things she doesn't speak about in detail, but her eyes glaze over when she mentions the search parties. She didn't sleep, she just worked, compartmentalizing the fear and the grief. Marco's calls went to voicemail. Her own home, they later found, was flooded and uninhabitable.

It wasn't until months later, when they were settled in a small rental apartment and a semblance of normalcy had returned, that the walls of her carefully constructed composure began to crumble. It started with the nightmares-vivid replays of the armory, the rising water, the feeling of being entombed. She would wake up gasping for air, drenched in sweat.

Now, any sudden, loud noise makes her flinch violently. A car backfiring sent her diving behind the couch last week, a reflexive action that left her feeling ashamed and foolish. She finds herself scanning every room she enters, checking exits, assessing structural integrity-a hypervigilance that serves her well on deployment but is exhausting in a grocery store. She's become irritable and distant. Marco tells me she barely speaks to him anymore, and when she does, her words are clipped and sharp. He says she spends hours just staring out the window, her body rigid with a tension he can't soothe. The other night, during a simple rain shower, he tried to put his arm around her, and she recoiled as if he'd burned her, shouting at him to leave her alone. She feels a profound, suffocating guilt-that she, the Sergeant, the one who was supposed to have everything under control, had been so utterly powerless.
